newsitem.title: UK: London palladium fixes at lowest level since 1993.
newsitem.headline: London palladium fixes at lowest level since 1993.

text.p: Palladium fell to a near three-year low on Wednesday after seeing its price erode for months on the back of steady Russian metal sales and sluggish Japanese electronics demand, dealers and analysts said.
The rare metal, used mainly in electronics and the motor industry, fixed in the afternoon at $122.25 an ounce, $1.75 below Tuesday's level and the lowest since December 1, 1993.
Prices closed in London at $122.00 per ounce, off 45 cents from the previous day.
"It looks absolutely terrible," a dealer said, adding that the metal could fall to $110 per ounce in coming weeks.
Palladium shed about $2 an ounce on Tuesday afternoon after investment funds and speculators started liquidating positions in the New York futures market, dealers said.
They attributed the selloff to the cumulative effect of bearish influences, rather than a specific market-moving factor.
The metal has been trending lower since rallying to around $145 an ounce in February, in line with rallies and subsequent declines in gold, silver and platinum.
A steady drip of selling has been seen from Russia, the world's largest producer, during the slack summer season when European industry was closed and demand was low, dealers said.
A fall in Japanese electronics industry demand earlier this year also led to lower palladium imports, analysts said. Palladium is used in computers, mobile phones and automotive electronics.

The problem stems from a build-up in inventory at the end of 1995, prompting manufacturers to scale back production in the first part of 1996, said Alison Cowley, a market research analyst at refiner Johnson Matthey.
"Now obviously that will have an impact upon palladium demand in capacitors and I think we're seeing that impact in the decline in palladium imports into Japan," she said.

Prices slumped last month to the lowest point since January 1994 after the market decided a new development in the car industry could hit demand. Palladium is a key element in catalytic converters, which neutralise toxic gases in car exhausts.

But growth in many parts of the electronics industry suggested demand would resume its uptrend eventually, Cowley said. Palladium demand in the auto industry was also expected to be strong, despite a lag in production.
The other precious metals were little changed from London's closing levels on Tuesday, and business was quiet.
Gold fixed in the afternoon at $383.50 an ounce, versus $383.10 on Tuesday afternoon, and dealers said it was likely to consolidate in the near term in a narrow $382-$385 band.
Bullion closed in London at $383.65, up 20 cents.

Dealers said gold was unlikely to make any significant move until after Friday's International Monetary Fund (IMF) meeting, which will discuss a plan to sell some IMF bullion reserves to aid poor nations.
"It's not going to go too far one way or the other until there's an decision on Friday to the IMF gold," one dealer said.
Silver finished at the same level as Tuesday's London close at $5.11 an ounce. Platinum, the sister metal of palladium, closed a touch easier $393.20, down 30 cents.
